name: Fragrance signature scent
lead: A signature scent is a single fragrance a person wears consistently, so that others come to link that smell with them. In appearance-focused communities it is treated as part of the overall impression, with scent counted alongside grooming, clothes and skin as something people notice when they meet someone. The idea is to be pleasant and memorable in close contact, where looks alone do not carry.

Perfume has a long history, from Mesopotamia and Egypt through Islamic and European perfumers, and modern fragrance families such as chypre, amber, floral, fougere, aquatic and gourmand each have well-known examples, such as Guerlain's Shalimar, Houbigant's Fougere Royale (1884) and Chanel No. 5, whose parfum dates to 1921 [1]. Perfumes are described as an accord of top notes that form the first impression, middle notes that make up the body, and base notes that appear around 30 minutes after application [1].

Research on smell and social judgment exists, though it has not tested signature scents as such. A 2026 systematic review of 21 studies concluded that odours act as often subconscious modulators of social judgments [2], and a 2025 study found that natural body odour was the least attractive of four modalities, face, body motion, voice and scent, to perceivers [3].

angle.text: Wearing one fragrance consistently is meant to add a pleasant, recognisable layer to a person's presence at close range. The recall claim comes from community discussion and has not been tested as such, while research shows odours can shape social judgments [2].

infobox: Parfum 15-30%, eau de parfum 15-20%, eau de toilette 5-15% [1]
About 2 to 4 hours for eau de toilette; up to 6 to 8 for parfum or eau de parfum [1]

paras: Wearers choose a fragrance family that suits them and wear it daily. Concentration terms describe the percentage of aromatic compounds and are imprecise because houses formulate differently. Wikipedia lists parfum or extrait at 15 to 30%, eau de parfum at 15 to 20%, eau de toilette at 5 to 15%, and eau de cologne at 2 to 3% [1].

How long a scent lasts depends on the wearer: Wikipedia notes that dry skin holds fragrance less well than oily skin, and that spicy or fatty foods and some medications can change how a fragrance smells [1].

Perfumery began in Mesopotamia, Egypt and the Indus Valley, and a Mesopotamian perfume maker named Tapputi appears on a second-millennium BC cuneiform tablet [1]. Al-Kindi wrote a work with over a hundred recipes in the 9th century, and eau de cologne developed from Giovanni Paolo Feminis's Aqua Admirabilis of 1693 [1]. Guerlain's Jicky (1889) is cited as the first fragrance labelled parfum, and synthetic aroma compounds such as vanillin and coumarin enabled new scents in the late 19th century [1].

A 2026 systematic review of 21 studies found that odours often act as subconscious modulators of social judgments, and that unpleasant odours can increase prejudice [2]. A 2026 experiment with 40 adults found that pleasant odours such as vanilla, rose, lavender and lemon changed pleasantness ratings of faces and other images, with effects that varied by scent and by the individual's emotional reaction to it [4]. A 2025 study in which 71 perceivers rated 61 people found that body odour was rated the least attractive of four modalities, with audio-video stimuli rated most attractive [3].

Wikipedia notes that natural fragrance materials may contain allergenic or carcinogenic compounds [1]. A 2026 survey of 461 women in the UAE reported that about 36% had health problems from fragrances and cosmetic products, most often respiratory problems, headaches and skin irritation [5].

No studies found on signature scents specifically. Related research is described above: odour and social judgment [2], ratings of body odour [3], and effects of pleasant odours on ratings of faces [4].

lore.intro: Signature scents are discussed in style and grooming communities as a way to be remembered.

claims.claim: A consistent signature scent makes you memorable
claims.believers: Proponents say people link a smell with a person and recall them through it.
claims.experts: No published study has tested signature scents on how people are remembered. A systematic review of 21 studies found odours act as often subconscious modulators of social judgments [2].

card.summary: Wearing one consistent fragrance so it becomes your identity; popular, untested.

quick.overview:
A signature scent is one fragrance worn consistently so others link it with you.

Communities treat it as a memorability tool.
quick.mechanism: Repeated exposure is said to build association between a smell and a person.
quick.risks: Fragrance ingredients can be allergenic; no studies on social effects were found.
